zh.summary: 以完整 Northstar 情境串聯釣魚分類、信任邊界、CEH 跨章知識、縱深防禦與事件證據，搭配五張原始 SVG 與四題白話參考解答。

sourceBody.text: Phishing · Spear Phishing · Whaling
Module 09：Social Engineering（社交工程）
這一課，我們不只要學會分辨三種釣魚攻擊，更要把之前學過的 CEH M01-01～M01-07，以及 M09-01 串成一套完整的資安知識體系。
課程脈絡補充：本文以「之前學過」串聯知識，是教材的敘事方式，不代表每位讀者已完成相關章節；尚未學過的概念可先了解用途，再透過文末連結補充。Northstar 與小林是教學用虛構情境，不是對真實事件或個人學習狀態的紀錄。
一、先建立最重要的觀念：攻擊者不一定要攻破電腦，也可以讓人替他開門
假設一間公司使用非常安全的雲端系統。
這間公司有：

items: 密碼保護及多因素驗證（MFA）。

sourceBody.text: 你可能認為：「公司有這麼多資安措施，應該很安全吧？」
但有一天，員工小林收到一封電子郵件：
小林您好，您負責的 Northstar 教材專案，合作廠商已完成最新修訂。
為避免影響明天的會議，請立即登入以下平台確認。
小林發現，寄件者知道自己的名字、專案名稱，甚至知道明天要開會。
他心想：「應該是真的吧？」
於是點進網站，輸入公司帳號和密碼。
問題來了。
攻擊者可能根本沒有突破公司的防火牆，而是讓小林主動把登入資料交給假網站。
這就是社交工程（Social Engineering）與釣魚攻擊（Phishing）的核心。
與上一課 M09-01 的連結
上一課我們學到：
信任一個人，不代表每個看起來像他的要求都已經獲得授權。
今天則進一步研究：
攻擊者如何利用這種信任，誘導人做出可能危害資訊安全的行為？
注意，輸入密碼代表可能發生憑證暴露，但不代表攻擊者一定成功登入。這個區別會在後面的事件調查中再次出現。
二、三種釣魚攻擊，其實是同一個概念的不同範圍
先記住這個關係：
Phishing（釣魚）⊃ Spear Phishing（魚叉式釣魚）⊃ Whaling（鯨釣）
也就是：

rows: 可以是不特定或特定對象
使用欺騙性訊息誘導危險行為
高階主管或其他高價值人物
被攻擊者的身分與價值

sourceBody.text: 這些分類符合 NIST、MITRE ATT&CK 及加拿大網路安全中心對釣魚與定向攻擊的說明。[NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/phishing)
來源補充｜NIST 的釣魚詞條提供多種依情境而定的定義；定向釣魚與鯨釣的目標區分，可直接對照[加拿大網路安全中心的分類](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/dont-take-bait-recognize-and-avoid-phishing-attacks)。本課的包含關係是便於理解的概念整理，不是三個機構共同發布的單一分類標準。
1. Phishing：像撒網捕魚
假設攻擊者寄出一萬封類似訊息：
「您的帳號即將停用，請立即登入驗證。」
他不一定知道收件者是誰。
只要有部分人相信，就有可能達到目的。
不過，大量寄送是常見做法，不是 Phishing 的必要定義。
2. Spear Phishing：像拿魚叉瞄準特定目標
攻擊者事先知道：

items: 小林正在處理 Northstar 專案。

sourceBody.text: 於是特別設計一封符合小林工作情境的訊息。
這就是魚叉式釣魚。
核心不是訊息有多逼真，而是有沒有針對特定目標進行設計。
3. Whaling：專門鎖定具有重要權限的人
假設攻擊者知道公司執行長可以存取董事會機密文件。
因此製作一封假冒董事會秘書的通知，專門寄給執行長，誘導他登入假網站。
這就是鯨釣攻擊。
但一定要注意：
假冒執行長 ≠ 鯨釣執行長。
如果攻擊者假冒執行長，要求一般財務承辦人匯款，攻擊對象仍然是財務承辦人。
這通常比較符合定向釣魚，也可能涉及商務電子郵件詐騙（Business Email Compromise, BEC）。
判斷 Whaling 時，不能把「冒充的身分」誤當成「實際被攻擊的對象」。
SVG 圖解 ①｜三種攻擊的包含關係

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02  /  視覺圖解 01 釣魚、魚叉式釣魚、鯨釣：看「攻擊目標」 三者是包含關係，不是三選一的平行分類。 PHISHING 釣魚 範圍最廣：用欺騙性訊息，誘導不安全行為。 常見：大量發送「帳號即將停用」通知。 SPEAR PHISHING 魚叉式釣魚 針對特定人、團隊或組織，量身設計內容。 例如：知道承辦人的專案與會議時間。 WHALING 鯨釣 瞄準高階、高價值目標，例如 CEO。 是魚叉式釣魚的一種。 ⚠ 常見誤解 寄件者顯示「執行長」 ↓ 收件者：財務承辦人 ≠ 自動判定為鯨釣 應該問的三個問題 ① 真正被鎖定的是誰？ ② 是否針對目標設計？ ③ 希望對方做什麼？ 判斷規則：冒充誰 ≠ 攻擊誰；金額大 ≠ 一定是鯨釣。
sourceBody.caption: 三種釣魚攻擊的包含關係｜使用者原始 SVG，圖中文字維持原樣。

sourceBody.text: 這張圖最重要的地方，是右側的「冒充誰」與「攻擊誰」。
例如，攻擊者假冒執行長，要求財務承辦人匯款，不能只因為訊息出現「執行長」就判定為 Whaling。
請記住：
Phishing 看欺騙行為，Spear Phishing 看目標是否經過特別挑選與設計，Whaling 則進一步看被鎖定的人物。 [NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/phishing)
三、把過去的 CEH 知識全部串起來
我們之前學過的 CEH 章節，其實是在回答同一個問題：
一個組織的重要資產，如何受到威脅，以及我們如何降低損害？
SVG 圖解 ②｜CEH 知識連結地圖

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02  /  視覺圖解 03 不是孤立章節：CEH 知識如何串成一條線？ 概念主軸：先知道保護什麼 → 再理解怎麼被攻擊 → 最後設計防護與應變。 01  保護什麼？ 02  攻擊如何發生？ 03  如何防護與復原？ M01-01  CIA 安全目標 機密性：不該看的人看不到 完整性、可用性也要保護 M01-02  風險四要素 資產：帳號、學員資料 威脅、弱點、風險：評估何者優先 M01-04  攻擊面／攻擊向量 郵件與登入頁是接觸點與途徑 M09-01 → M09-02  信任到釣魚 冒名、壓力、假入口與目標分類 M01-05  Kill Chain／ATT&CK T1566：釣魚可作為初始存取手法 M01-06  縱深防禦 查證、MFA、權限控管 過濾與監控：一道失效還有下一道 M01-07  風險管理／事件應變 通報、止損、調查、復原 以證據區分「收到」與「遭入侵」 M01-03｜合法授權與 ROE：這是所有調查、測試與演練共同遵守的邊界。 核心思考：資產 → 攻擊入口 → 誘導行為 → 安全控制 → 證據與復原。
sourceBody.caption: CEH 跨章節知識連結地圖｜使用者原始 SVG，圖中文字維持原樣。

sourceBody.text: 我們沿著圖中的方向，重新理解已經學過的知識。
第一層：M01-01｜CIA Triad
CIA Triad 是資訊安全最基本的三項目標：

items: Confidentiality（機密性）：不應該知道資訊的人，不能取得資訊。
Integrity（完整性）：資訊不能受到未授權的變更。
Availability（可用性）：有權使用的人，需要時能正常使用。

sourceBody.text: 現在把它套到釣魚攻擊。
假設攻擊者透過假網站取得小林的密碼，接著成功登入公司帳號，下載機密文件。
主要影響的是什麼？
Confidentiality，機密性。
如果攻擊者進一步修改教材中的收款帳戶，可能又會影響 Integrity（完整性）。
如果攻擊者透過惡意附件部署勒索軟體，使平台無法運作，就可能影響 Availability（可用性）。
一個釣魚事件可能影響不只一項 CIA 目標。
但要注意：CIA 是資訊安全的分析框架，並不涵蓋所有商業損失，例如詐騙造成的直接金錢損失。
第二層：M01-02｜Asset、Threat、Vulnerability、Risk
上一課我們曾用咖啡廳和教材平台學過這四個名詞。
現在繼續用 Northstar：

rows: 公司帳號、教材、學員個資
攻擊者利用假訊息取得帳密
缺乏獨立查證程序、採用易遭釣魚的驗證方式
帳號遭冒用、個資外洩及其發生可能性與影響

sourceBody.text: 這裡有個重要的觀念。
釣魚攻擊不一定需要軟體漏洞。
假設 Northstar 網站沒有程式漏洞，但員工習慣直接使用電子郵件提供的登入連結。
這種不安全的工作習慣與流程，就可能成為攻擊者利用的弱點。
因此，Vulnerability 不只指程式碼中的安全缺陷，也可以是流程、設定與控制措施不足。
第三層：M01-04｜Attack Surface 與 Attack Vector
這是今天很重要的一個跨章節連結。
我們以前說：
Attack Surface（攻擊面）是在問：
「組織有哪些地方可能受到接觸或攻擊？」
Attack Vector（攻擊向量）是在問：
「攻擊者可能透過什麼途徑下手？」
在 Northstar 的案例：
電子郵件系統、員工使用的通訊平台，以及需要處理外部訊息的工作流程，都可能構成攻擊面的一部分。
而攻擊者寄送假冒合作廠商的訊息，誘導員工進入假登入網站，就是一條攻擊向量。
你可以這樣理解：
攻擊面是可能接觸到的地方；攻擊向量是攻擊者利用那些地方的具體途徑。
但「有攻擊面」不代表「有漏洞」，更不代表「攻擊成功」。
第四層：M01-05｜Cyber Kill Chain 與 MITRE ATT&CK
這裡我們可以更進一步。
MITRE ATT&CK 是用來整理真實世界中攻擊者戰術（Tactics）與技術（Techniques）的知識庫。
目前 ATT&CK Enterprise 將 Phishing 列為：
T1566 — Phishing
並歸在 Initial Access（初始存取）戰術之下。
T1566 還包括以下技術分類：

rows: 透過第三方服務傳遞釣魚訊息
利用語音進行定向釣魚

sourceBody.text: 這是 MITRE ATT&CK 所使用的技術分類，不等於所有釣魚詐騙的完整分類。尤其是單純誘騙轉帳的案件，不一定涉及攻擊者取得系統的初始存取權限。[MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/)
試著回想 M01-05：
Cyber Kill Chain 幫我們理解整體攻擊過程；MITRE ATT&CK 則幫我們描述具體的攻擊行為。
當調查人員發現某員工收到有針對性的惡意連結時，可以把它與 T1566.002 連結，進一步檢查是否發生帳密外洩、異常登入或其他後續行為。
但不能只看到釣魚訊息，就直接認定攻擊者已經取得系統存取權。
四、理解釣魚攻擊真正的核心：Trust Boundary
現在要介紹一個資訊工程與資安架構設計中非常重要的概念：
Trust Boundary（信任邊界）
什麼是信任邊界？
想像你家門口有一位陌生人。
他說自己是你的朋友介紹來的，而且知道你朋友的姓名。
這些資訊可以幫助你判斷，但還不足以證明他的身分。
如果你直接把鑰匙交給他，就是讓尚未驗證的人取得原本受到保護的資源。
資訊系統也有類似的邊界。
例如：
外部電子郵件是未經信任的資訊來源。
公司帳號與內部文件是受到保護的資產。
當外部郵件要求員工提供密碼、變更權限或付款時，就是要求員工跨越某種安全界線。
SVG 圖解 ③｜從冒名到可能損害的因果流程

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02  /  視覺圖解 02 攻擊者如何利用信任，讓人跨越安全界線？ 從「看起來可信」到「可能損害」，中間有多個可阻斷的節點。 ① 冒用身分 假裝合作廠商 或公司主管 ② 補上背景 正確提到姓名 專案或近期活動 ③ 提出要求 要求登入 開附件或改匯款 ④ 跨越界線 對未驗證網站 輸入帳密／付款 ⑤ 可能後果 帳號遭冒用 或款項受損 信任界線 / Trust Boundary ✓ 正確的阻斷方式 不採用訊息提供的聯絡方式。 從原本就知道的官方管道查證。 先確認身分、要求與授權範圍。 ! 沒有查證時的風險 可能洩露登入憑證、執行惡意檔案， 或造成錯誤付款；後果並非必然發生。 收到信件 ≠ 已經遭到入侵。 本圖是教學用的因果模型，並非官方固定攻擊步驟。

sourceBody.text: 請仔細看圖中的第三個步驟：
「要求登入、開附件或改匯款。」
這個步驟之所以重要，是因為攻擊者真正想達成的目的，往往不是讓你閱讀訊息。
而是希望你採取某個行動。
例如：
情境 A：要求重新登入
攻擊者希望員工把登入資訊輸入假網站，可能導致帳密遭竊。
情境 B：要求打開附件
攻擊者希望員工開啟惡意檔案，可能藉此執行惡意程式。
情境 C：要求更改匯款帳號
攻擊者希望財務人員將原本應匯給廠商的款項轉入其他帳戶。
這三個情境的共同點，是利用看似合理的訊息誘導危險行動。
但三者的直接目標不同，因此所需的防護方式也不同。
例如，防釣魚 MFA 能保護登入流程，卻不能直接阻止一名已合法登入的財務人員，被假指示誘導而主動匯款。
這也是為什麼我們不能把資安防護等同於「安裝某一套軟體」。
五、M01-06｜為什麼需要縱深防禦？
之前學過的 Defense in Depth（縱深防禦），在這一課非常重要。
它的意思是：
當一道防線失效，後面還有其他不同功能的防線，可以繼續防護、偵測或限制損害。
SVG 圖解 ④｜五道不同功能的防線

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02  /  視覺圖解 04 M01-06 縱深防禦：五道不同功能的防線 只靠員工辨識錯字不夠。防護應分散在技術、流程、權限與應變各層。 01 訊息入口 SPF／DKIM／DMARC、附件與網址過濾 限制偽冒寄件來源；但無法證明每一項商業要求都是真的。 預防 02 人員查證 使用原有電話或正式入口獨立確認 不使用可疑訊息附的客服電話、網址或 QR code。 阻斷 03 業務流程 改匯款帳號、付款或權限變更需雙重核准 即使真的收到主管指示，也要走既有核准程序。 限制 04 帳號與權限 FIDO2／Passkey、最小權限、異常登入警示 降低憑證被濫用的風險；不能取代匯款查證。 限制／偵測 05 通報與事件應變 快速通報、保全證據、撤銷工作階段 降低傷害並釐清影響；看不到紀錄不代表沒發生。 回應 設計原則：不同防線要能互補；單一控制無法完全消除社交工程風險。
sourceBody.caption: 釣魚攻擊的五道縱深防禦｜使用者原始 SVG，圖中文字維持原樣。

sourceBody.text: 這裡特別深入兩項初學者應該認識的技術。
1. SPF、DKIM、DMARC 是什麼？
這三項都是電子郵件安全領域的重要機制。
SPF（Sender Policy Framework）主要用來確認寄信伺服器是否獲得網域授權。
DKIM（DomainKeys Identified Mail）利用數位簽章，協助驗證郵件是否經過對應網域的簽署，以及簽署內容是否受到更改。
DMARC（Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance）則結合驗證結果與寄件網域對齊規則，讓網域擁有者指定收件方如何處理驗證失敗的郵件，並取得相關報告。

技術補充｜SPF 檢查的是 SMTP 信封寄件者等網域，不是只看畫面上的寄件者名稱；DMARC 通過需要 SPF 或 DKIM 至少一項通過，且相應網域與 From 網域對齊。網域政策是處理建議，最終處置仍由收件方綜合判斷。現行 [RFC 9989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9989.html)（2026 年 5 月）已取代 RFC 7489；驗證通過仍不等於內容或付款要求合法。
它們能協助降低網域偽冒風險。[MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/)
但它們不是萬能的。
假設攻擊者真的入侵合作廠商的電子郵件帳號，再透過該帳號寄信給你。
即使郵件通過 SPF、DKIM、DMARC 驗證，也不代表郵件中的要求一定合法。
驗證郵件來源，不等於驗證商業要求。
2. MFA 與 Passkey 有什麼不同？
MFA（Multi-Factor Authentication，多因素驗證）是要求使用者提供不同類型的驗證因素。
例如密碼加上手機驗證碼。
這通常比只有密碼更安全。
但你可能會問：
「如果攻擊者連驗證碼一起騙走，怎麼辦？」
這就是傳統 OTP（One-Time Password，一次性密碼）驗證的一項限制。
攻擊者可能即時轉送使用者輸入的驗證碼。
因此，我們會進一步考慮：
Phishing-Resistant MFA（抗釣魚多因素驗證）
例如正確實作的 FIDO2／WebAuthn 驗證。
其重要特性是將驗證過程與合法網站的網域進行密碼學上的綁定，使假網站難以取得可直接用於真正網站登入的有效驗證結果。
NIST SP 800-63B-4 明確指出，手動輸入的一次性驗證碼不屬於抗釣魚驗證；WebAuthn 則能透過驗證者名稱綁定，提供抗釣魚能力。[NIST Pages](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html)
技術補充｜「抗釣魚」與「多因素」是不同性質。Passkey 使用公私鑰驗證；若要作為多因素驗證，還要正確要求並驗證 PIN 或生物辨識等本機啟用因素，不能只看到 FIDO2／WebAuthn 名稱就認定已符合 MFA。[NIST SP 800-63B-4，第 3.1.7 與 3.2.5 節](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html)
不過，Passkey 也不是可以阻止所有網路詐騙的萬能工具。
它主要處理登入驗證安全，無法直接驗證付款要求的真實性，更不能取代組織內部的權限與核准程序。
這裡的工程設計重點
假設 Northstar 要改善資安，你不應該只提出：
「請所有員工提高警覺。」
比較完整的設計是：
公司透過郵件安全機制過濾部分偽冒訊息；重要操作需要獨立查證；帳號使用抗釣魚 MFA；敏感資料採最小權限原則；高風險付款需要獨立核准；系統保留必要的稽核紀錄。
這些防線互相補足，才比較接近 M01-06 的核心精神。
六、M01-07｜如何判斷釣魚攻擊是否真的成功？
接下來切換成資安事件調查人員的視角。
假設 Northstar 的小林說：
「我昨天好像點到一封奇怪的信。」
這時候，調查人員應該怎麼做？
最容易出現的錯誤，就是直接寫：
「小林遭到釣魚攻擊，公司帳號已遭入侵。」
這個結論可能超出目前證據能支持的範圍。

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02  /  視覺圖解 05 M01-07 事件應變：不要把「收到」直接寫成「入侵」 安全事件判斷要把「觀察」「推論」「驗證」分開，逐層查證。 ① 收到訊息 可查證的證據： 郵件紀錄或畫面 不能直接推論： 只證明送達 ② 點了連結 可查證的證據： 使用者陳述、瀏覽紀錄 不能直接推論： 不等於執行惡意程式 ③ 輸入帳密 可查證的證據： 本人陳述、登入頁紀錄 不能直接推論： 屬可能憑證暴露 ④ 可疑登入 可查證的證據： 身分平台稽核紀錄 不能直接推論： 不等於已經外洩資料 ⑤ 資料被取用 可查證的證據： 存取／下載／外傳紀錄 不能直接推論： 查明內容與範圍 懷疑已經發生釣魚事件，先做哪些事？ 1 停止可疑操作 2 依流程通報資安窗口 3 由負責人處置帳號與裝置 4 保留紀錄並調查影響 現場重點：不自行反覆開啟可疑檔案；紀錄與處置依組織授權及程序執行。

sourceBody.text: 這張圖的五個階段非常重要。
閱讀圖解提醒｜這五項是用來區分「目前證據能確認什麼」的檢查點，不是每起事件都會依序走完的固定流程。例如，假冒主管的匯款詐騙可能沒有輸入帳密或異常登入；調查也可能先從付款異常或資料存取告警開始，再回查前因。
第一階段：收到訊息
可以確認的是，有訊息送達員工。
但還不知道員工是否閱讀、點擊或執行任何操作。
第二階段：點擊連結
如果員工說自己點過連結，應該記錄他的陳述，並利用可取得的瀏覽紀錄與安全日誌交叉查證。
單純點擊，不代表一定執行了惡意程式。
第三階段：輸入帳密
如果員工確認自己在可疑網站輸入帳密，應視為可能發生憑證暴露，立即依組織程序處置。
但不能直接推論攻擊者已成功登入。
第四階段：發現可疑登入
如果身分驗證平台出現異常登入活動，就需要調查來源、時間、使用的驗證方式、工作階段與後續操作。
注意：
「異常登入」也可能有其他解釋，例如本人使用新裝置或不同網路。
必須透過更多證據確認。
第五階段：資料被存取或轉出
假設確認某帳號曾在異常時段下載公司文件。
接下來需要調查下載的是哪些文件、數量、時間，以及是否存在外傳證據。
證據能支持到哪裡，結論就寫到哪裡。
這項原則也與 MITRE ATT&CK 的釣魚偵測思路相符：應交叉分析郵件、檔案、程序執行、網路活動及身分驗證紀錄，而不是只憑單一事件下結論。[MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0070/)
如果真的發現自己輸入了密碼，怎麼辦？
應立即停止可疑操作，透過原本可信任的管道通報資安窗口。
由負責人依風險處理帳號，例如從可信任的裝置更改密碼、撤銷可疑工作階段、檢查 MFA 設定，以及調查相關日誌。
若涉及匯款，應立即聯絡銀行及組織的財務或反詐處理窗口，爭取阻止或追回款項。
不要為了確認可疑附件是否有問題，就自行反覆開啟或執行。
七、再把 M09-01 與 M09-02 連起來
現在回到整個 Module 09 的學習主軸。
在 M09-01，我們已經學過：
社交工程利用人的信任、權威感、急迫感或其他心理與社會因素，誘導人做出特定行為。
到了 M09-02，我們進一步看到：
攻擊者可以藉由電子郵件、通訊軟體及其他數位管道，把這些心理因素包裝成具有欺騙性的訊息。
而釣魚攻擊也不只有電子郵件。
例如：
Smishing 是利用簡訊進行的釣魚；Vishing 是利用語音通話進行的釣魚；Quishing 則利用 QR Code 引導使用者進入釣魚情境。
不過，辨識這些名稱不是最重要的能力。
真正重要的是：
不論攻擊者使用文字、聲音、圖片或 QR Code，你都能辨認訊息來源、要求的行動，以及安全界線在哪裡。
加拿大網路安全中心也建議，遇到可疑要求時，應透過獨立且可信任的管道核實，而不是使用可疑訊息中提供的聯絡資訊。[Canadian Centre for Cyber Security](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/dont-take-bait-recognize-and-avoid-phishing-attacks)
還有一個值得補充的細節：
HTTPS 與瀏覽器鎖頭圖示，不等於網站一定是合法公司經營。
HTTPS 主要保護瀏覽器與所連線網站之間的通訊；詐騙網站同樣可以使用 HTTPS。
因此，網站具有加密連線，也不能取代身分、網域及交易要求的驗證。
八、從初學者提升到資安工程師：要培養什麼判斷能力？
學完今天這一課，我希望你建立的是一套能反覆使用的分析方法，而不只是記住三個英文名詞。
當你遇到疑似釣魚事件時，可以從五個問題切入：

rows: 2. 攻擊者利用什麼入口與途徑？
3. 如何利用人的信任誘導行動？
4. 哪些控制措施可以阻擋或限制損害？
5. 有哪些證據可以確認事件進展？

sourceBody.text: 而 M01-03 的合法授權與 ROE（Rules of Engagement，交戰規則），則是所有資安測試與調查都必須遵守的前提。
即使只是進行教育訓練的模擬釣魚演練，也應事先取得適當授權，確認測試範圍、資料處理方式及通報程序。
今天最值得記住的核心觀念
攻擊者利用信任，引導人做出可能跨越安全界線的行動；防守者則必須透過驗證、權限控管、流程設計及事件調查，阻斷或限制可能的損害。
這個原則不只適用於釣魚攻擊。
未來學習帳號冒用、權限提升、惡意程式、網頁應用程式安全，甚至 AI Agent Security，都可以繼續使用這套思考方式。
九、理解檢核｜請試著用自己的話回答
這次使用教材原本的 Northstar 案例，不先提供標準答案。
網站編輯補充：下方提供可自行對照的白話參考解答，預設收合，保留先自行思考的順序；這不代表讀者已提交作答或完成理解驗證。
情境：
Northstar 的一般財務承辦人收到一封電子郵件。
寄件者顯示為公司執行長，信件正確提到近期教材專案，要求財務承辦人將款項改匯到新帳戶。
寄件者還強調：
「我現在正在開會，不要打電話，請直接處理。」
目前只知道承辦人收到訊息，尚未確認是否依照指示匯款。
問題 A｜攻擊分類
如果確認這是惡意訊息，你會把它分類成 Phishing、Spear Phishing，還是 Whaling？
請說明判斷的依據，特別注意「冒充誰」與「攻擊誰」的差異。
問題 B｜安全控制措施
承辦人發現信件知道正確的專案名稱。
這能證明寄件者是真正的執行長嗎？
如果你是公司的資安工程師，你會要求承辦人透過什麼方式查證？又會設計什麼機制降低類似事件的風險？
問題 C｜證據與事件應變
目前只能證明財務承辦人收到訊息。
你能直接在事件調查報告寫下「公司已遭詐騙並損失款項」嗎？
你還需要取得哪些證據？
進階問題 D｜跨章節整合
假設調查後確認公司真的發生錯誤匯款。
請使用 M01-02 的 Asset、Threat、Vulnerability、Risk 四個概念分析這起事件，再提出兩項符合 M01-06 縱深防禦精神的改善措施。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 A 參考解答｜分類要看真正被鎖定的人
paragraphs: 若已確認是惡意訊息，最貼切的是 Spear Phishing（魚叉式釣魚），同時也屬於廣義的 Phishing（釣魚）。訊息針對特定財務承辦人的工作情境，還使用正確專案資訊提高可信度。
不能只因寄件者冒充執行長，就把它叫作 Whaling（鯨釣）。本題被鎖定的是一般財務承辦人，不是執行長；「冒充誰」與「要騙誰」是兩件事。這也可能屬於 BEC 類型的付款詐騙，但是否已造成款項損失，要另看付款證據。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 B 參考解答｜知道背景不等於要求已獲授權
paragraphs: 不能。專案名稱可能來自公開資訊、外洩資料或遭冒用的合作帳號。內容正確只是線索，不能單獨證明現在發出要求的人是誰，更不能證明這次付款變更已獲核准。
先暫停改帳戶或匯款，使用公司原本的通訊錄、已核實的電話或既有內部系統，向本人與負責付款核准的人查證這個具體要求。不要使用可疑郵件新提供的電話、連結或回覆管道來證明它自己是真的；「我在開會」不能取代必要查證。
流程上可要求收款帳戶變更須獨立回撥確認，並由另一位有權限的人覆核；系統則保留變更與核准紀錄，搭配適當付款限額或異常提醒。郵件驗證與抗釣魚 MFA 可以補強防線，但不能取代對付款要求本身的核實。

sourceBody.summary: 問題 C 參考解答｜收到訊息，不等於已經損失款項
paragraphs: 還不能。現在只知道財務承辦人收到訊息，不能直接寫成已匯款、已遭詐騙或帳號已被入侵。初步紀錄可以寫：「收到疑似定向釣魚訊息；是否變更付款資料及實際付款，仍待確認。」
接著保存原始郵件與時間資訊，查核承辦人的回覆、收款帳戶變更、付款申請、核准紀錄，以及銀行的實際交易與款項狀態。還要比對原本正確的收款對象，確認是否真的匯到非預期帳戶。提出申請、通過核准與完成匯款，不能混成同一件事。
若已確認發生可疑匯款，應依組織流程立即通知財務、資安與銀行處理，並持續保存證據；是否能攔阻或追回款項，仍待銀行與後續調查確認。

sourceBody.summary: 進階問題 D 參考解答｜用資產、威脅、弱點與風險串起防禦
paragraphs: Asset（資產）：公司的款項、正確的收款帳戶資料，以及付款流程與核准紀錄。Threat（威脅）：攻擊者假冒主管，企圖把合法付款導向他控制的帳戶。
Vulnerability（弱點）：可以優先調查是否缺少獨立查證、帳戶變更覆核或職務分工；這些是待查的可能弱點，不能只因已發生錯誤匯款，就認定每一項流程都不存在。Risk（風險）：在這些條件下，款項被錯誤移轉的可能性與損失影響；本題已確認的錯誤匯款，則是實際發生的事件與影響，不能拿它直接算出未來發生機率。
第一道改善：收款帳戶變更前，用既有可信管道向真正的廠商或授權負責人獨立確認，並留下核實紀錄。這是在錯誤指示進入付款流程之前攔阻。
第二道改善：付款系統由不同人覆核與核准高風險變更，搭配限額及即時交易提醒。即使前面的查證失效，後面仍有核准、偵測與減少損害的機制。這就是分層互補，而不是只重複提醒員工小心。

sourceBody.text: Phishing · Spear Phishing · Whaling
Module 09: Social Engineering

In this lesson, we will not only learn to distinguish three types of phishing attack, but also connect CEH M01-01 through M01-07 and M09-01, which we studied earlier, into a complete framework of cybersecurity knowledge.

Curriculum context: references to what was “previously learned” connect the ideas in the teaching narrative; they do not establish that every reader has completed those topics. If a concept is new, first understand its role and use the links at the end to explore it. Northstar and Lin are fictional teaching scenarios, not records of a real incident or a person’s learning progress.
1. Start with the most important idea: attackers do not always need to break into a computer; they can get someone to open the door for them
Suppose a company uses a very secure cloud system.
This company has:

items: Controls over permissions to access data.

sourceBody.text: You might think, “With all these security measures, the company should be very safe, right?”
But one day, an employee named Lin receives an email:
Hello Lin, our partner vendor has completed the latest revisions for the Northstar teaching-materials project you are responsible for.
To avoid disrupting tomorrow’s meeting, please sign in to the platform below immediately to confirm.
Lin notices that the sender knows his name and the project name, and even knows about tomorrow’s meeting.
He thinks, “It must be genuine, right?”
So he opens the website and enters his company username and password.
Here is the problem.
The attacker may never have breached the company’s firewall at all. Instead, the attacker persuaded Lin to hand his login information to a fake website.
This is the core of social engineering and phishing.
Connection to the previous lesson, M09-01
In the previous lesson, we learned:
Trusting someone does not mean that every request appearing to come from that person has been authorized.
Today, we will explore a further question:
How do attackers exploit that trust to persuade people to take actions that may harm information security?

Note that entering a password means credentials may have been exposed; it does not mean the attacker necessarily signed in successfully. This distinction will come up again when we discuss incident investigation.
2. The three types of phishing are different scopes of the same concept
First, remember this relationship:
Phishing ⊃ Spear Phishing ⊃ Whaling
In other words:

rows: Using deceptive messages to induce dangerous behavior
魚叉式釣魚、定向釣魚 (spear phishing, targeted phishing)
A specific individual, team, or organization
Designing the message for the target
Senior executives or other high-value individuals
The identity and value of the person being targeted

sourceBody.text: These categories are consistent with explanations of phishing and targeted attacks from NIST, MITRE ATT&CK, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. [NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/phishing)

Source clarification | NIST lists context-dependent definitions of phishing. For the target distinction between spear phishing and whaling, see the [Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s classification](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/dont-take-bait-recognize-and-avoid-phishing-attacks). The nested relationship here is a teaching aid, not a single classification standard jointly issued by all three organizations.
1. Phishing: like casting a fishing net
Suppose an attacker sends ten thousand similar messages:
“Your account is about to be disabled. Sign in immediately to verify it.”
The attacker does not necessarily know who the recipients are.
If even some recipients believe the message, the attacker may achieve the intended goal.
However, sending messages in bulk is a common practice, not a required part of the definition of phishing.
2. Spear Phishing: like aiming a spear at a specific target
The attacker already knows:

items: Lin is responsible for teaching materials.
Lin is working on the Northstar project.

sourceBody.text: The attacker therefore designs a message specifically suited to Lin’s work context.
This is spear phishing.
The key is not how realistic the message looks, but whether it was designed for a specific target.
3. Whaling: specifically targeting people with important privileges
Suppose an attacker knows that the company’s CEO can access confidential board documents.
The attacker therefore creates a notice impersonating the board secretary and sends it specifically to the CEO, trying to get the CEO to sign in to a fake website.
This is a whaling attack.
But be sure to note:
Impersonating a CEO ≠ targeting a CEO with whaling.
If an attacker impersonates the CEO and asks an ordinary finance staff member to transfer money, the person being targeted is still the finance staff member.
This generally fits targeted phishing more closely and may also involve Business Email Compromise (BEC).
When identifying whaling, do not confuse “the identity being impersonated” with “the person actually being targeted.”

PHISHING The broadest category: using deceptive messages to induce unsafe behavior. A common example: mass-sent notices claiming that an account will soon be disabled. SPEAR PHISHING Content tailored to a specific person, team or organization. For example, knowing the staff member’s project and meeting schedule. WHALING Targets senior or high-value people, such as a CEO. A type of spear phishing. Warning: a common misconception The displayed sender is “CEO”. ↓ The recipient is a finance staff member. This does not automatically make it whaling. Three questions to ask ① Who is actually being targeted? ② Was the message designed for that target? ③ What action does the sender want the recipient to take? Classification rule: the identity impersonated is not the person attacked; a large sum does not necessarily mean whaling.

sourceBody.text: The most important part of this diagram is the distinction on the right between “who is being impersonated” and “who is being targeted.”
For example, if an attacker impersonates the CEO and asks a finance staff member to transfer money, the mere appearance of “CEO” in the message does not make it whaling.
Remember:

For phishing, look for deception. For spear phishing, ask whether the target was specifically selected and the message tailored. For whaling, look further at the person being targeted. [NIST Computer Security Resource Center](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/phishing)
3. Connect all the CEH knowledge we have learned
The CEH chapters we studied earlier are actually answering the same question:
How are an organization’s important assets threatened, and how can we reduce the harm?

sourceBody.text: Let us follow the direction in the diagram to revisit the knowledge we have already learned.
First layer: M01-01 | CIA Triad
The CIA Triad consists of the three most basic information-security objectives:

items: Confidentiality: people who should not know the information must not be able to obtain it.
Integrity: information must not be changed without authorization.
Availability: authorized users must be able to use the resource normally when they need it.

sourceBody.text: Now apply this to a phishing attack.
Suppose an attacker obtains Lin’s password through a fake website, then successfully signs in to his company account and downloads confidential documents.
Which objective is primarily affected?
Confidentiality.
If the attacker then changes the payment account listed in the teaching materials, integrity may also be affected.
If the attacker deploys ransomware through a malicious attachment and prevents the platform from operating, availability may be affected.
A phishing incident may affect more than one CIA objective.
But note that CIA is a framework for analyzing information security. It does not cover every type of business loss, such as direct financial losses caused by fraud.
Second layer: M01-02 | Asset, Threat, Vulnerability, Risk
In the previous lesson, we used a café and a teaching platform to learn these four terms.
Let us continue with Northstar:

headers: How it applies to a phishing attack
rows: Company accounts, teaching materials, and learners’ personal data
An attacker using fake messages to obtain usernames and passwords
Lack of an independent verification procedure; use of authentication methods susceptible to phishing
Account impersonation and personal-data disclosure, together with their likelihood and impact

sourceBody.text: There is an important idea here.
A phishing attack does not necessarily require a software vulnerability.
Suppose the Northstar website has no software vulnerabilities, but employees habitually use the sign-in links provided in emails directly.
These unsafe work habits and processes can become weaknesses that an attacker exploits.
A vulnerability therefore does not refer only to a security flaw in code. It can also be a deficiency in processes, configurations, or controls.
Third layer: M01-04 | Attack Surface and Attack Vector
This is an especially important connection between chapters in today’s lesson.
Earlier, we said:
Attack Surface asks:
“Which parts of the organization could be contacted or attacked?”
Attack Vector asks:
“What route might an attacker use to attack?”
In the Northstar example:
The email system, the messaging platforms employees use, and workflows that handle external messages can all form part of the attack surface.
An attacker sending a message that impersonates a partner vendor and directs an employee to a fake sign-in website is an attack vector.
You can think of it this way:
The attack surface consists of the places that can be reached; an attack vector is the specific route an attacker uses through those places.
But “having an attack surface” does not mean “having a vulnerability,” much less “a successful attack.”
Fourth layer: M01-05 | Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK
We can take this a step further.
MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base that organizes the tactics and techniques used by attackers in the real world.
ATT&CK Enterprise currently lists phishing as:
T1566 — Phishing
It is classified under the Initial Access tactic.
T1566 also includes the following technique categories:

rows: Delivering phishing messages through a third-party service
Using voice communication for targeted phishing

sourceBody.text: These are the technique categories used by MITRE ATT&CK, not a complete classification of all phishing scams. In particular, a case that only tricks someone into transferring money does not necessarily involve an attacker gaining initial access to a system. [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/)
Try recalling M01-05:
The Cyber Kill Chain helps us understand the overall attack process; MITRE ATT&CK helps us describe specific attacker behaviors.

When investigators discover that an employee received a targeted malicious link, they can relate it to T1566.002 and then check for exposed credentials, unusual sign-ins, or other subsequent activity.
But seeing a phishing message alone does not justify concluding that the attacker has already gained system access.
4. Understand the real core of phishing: the Trust Boundary
We now introduce a very important concept in computer engineering and security architecture design:
Trust Boundary
What is a trust boundary?
Imagine a stranger standing at your front door.
He says a friend of yours referred him, and he knows your friend’s name.
That information may help you assess the situation, but it is not enough to prove his identity.
If you hand him your key straight away, you are giving an unverified person access to a resource that was previously protected.
Information systems have similar boundaries.
For example:
External email is an untrusted source of information.
Company accounts and internal documents are protected assets.
When an external email asks employees to provide passwords, change permissions, or make a payment, it is asking them to cross a security boundary of some kind.
SVG diagram ③ | The causal path from impersonation to possible harm

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02 / Visual diagram 02 How do attackers exploit trust to make people cross a security boundary? Between “looks trustworthy” and “possible harm” are several points where the chain can be interrupted. ① Impersonate an identity Pretend to be a partner vendor or a company manager. ② Add background details Correctly mention a name, a project or recent activity. ③ Make a request Ask the recipient to log in, open an attachment or change a payment destination. ④ Cross the boundary At an unverified website, enter credentials or make a payment. ⑤ Possible consequences An account is misused or money is lost. Trust Boundary ✓ The right way to interrupt the chain Do not use the contact information provided in the message. Verify through an official channel you already know. First confirm the identity, the request and the scope of authorization. ! Risks when verification is skipped Credentials may be exposed, malicious files may be executed, or an incorrect payment may occur; these outcomes are not inevitable. Receiving an email does not mean a compromise has already occurred. This diagram is a causal model for teaching, not an official fixed sequence of attack steps.

sourceBody.text: Look carefully at the third step in the diagram:
“Ask the person to sign in, open an attachment, or change a payment.”
This step matters because the attacker’s actual goal is often not simply to have you read a message.
Instead, the attacker wants you to take a particular action.
For example:
Scenario A: asking someone to sign in again
The attacker wants the employee to enter login information on a fake website, potentially leading to stolen credentials.
Scenario B: asking someone to open an attachment
The attacker wants the employee to open a malicious file, potentially causing malicious code to execute.
Scenario C: asking someone to change the payment account
The attacker wants finance staff to transfer money intended for the vendor into a different account.
All three scenarios use a seemingly reasonable message to induce a dangerous action.
But their immediate objectives differ, so the protections needed also differ.

For example, phishing-resistant MFA can protect the sign-in process, but it cannot directly stop a finance employee who is already legitimately signed in from willingly transferring money after being misled by a false instruction.
This is also why we cannot equate cybersecurity protection with “installing a particular piece of software.”
5. M01-06 | Why do we need defense in depth?
Defense in Depth, which we studied earlier, is especially important in this lesson.
It means:
When one defensive layer fails, other layers with different functions remain behind it to continue protecting, detecting, or limiting harm.
SVG diagram ④ | Five defensive layers with different functions

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02 / Visual diagram 04 M01-06 Defense in depth: five lines of defense with different functions Relying only on staff to spot typos is not enough. Protection should span technology, processes, permissions and response. 01 Message entry points SPF / DKIM / DMARC, attachment filtering and URL filtering. Limit sender-domain impersonation, but do not prove that every business request is genuine. Prevent 02 Human verification Independently confirm using an existing phone number or official entry point. Do not use support numbers, URLs or QR codes supplied in a suspicious message. Interrupt 03 Business processes Require dual approval for payment-account changes, payments or permission changes. Follow the established approval process even when instructions genuinely come from a manager. Limit 04 Accounts and permissions FIDO2 / Passkey, least privilege and unusual-login alerts. Reduce credential-misuse risk; these controls do not replace payment verification. Limit / detect 05 Reporting and incident response Promptly report, preserve evidence and revoke sessions. Reduce harm and establish the impact; not seeing a record does not mean nothing happened. Respond Design principle: different defenses should complement one another; no single control can completely eliminate social-engineering risk.

sourceBody.text: Here we take a closer look at two technical areas that beginners should understand.
1. What are SPF, DKIM, and DMARC?
All three are important mechanisms in email security.
SPF (Sender Policy Framework) primarily checks whether a sending mail server is authorized by the domain.
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) uses digital signatures to help verify whether an email was signed by the corresponding domain and whether the signed content has been changed.

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) combines authentication results with sender-domain alignment rules, allowing domain owners to specify how recipients should handle messages that fail authentication and to receive related reports.

Technical clarification | SPF checks an SMTP domain such as the envelope-sender domain, not merely the displayed sender name. A DMARC pass requires SPF or DKIM to pass with the relevant domain aligned to the From domain. The published policy requests handling; the receiver makes the final decision using additional analysis. [RFC 9989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9989.html), published in May 2026, supersedes RFC 7489. Passing authentication still does not establish that the content or payment request is legitimate.
They can help reduce the risk of domain impersonation. [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/)
But they are not a cure-all.
Suppose an attacker actually compromises a partner vendor’s email account and then sends you an email from that account.
Even if the email passes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks, that does not mean its request is necessarily legitimate.
Verifying the source of an email is not the same as verifying a business request.
2. How do MFA and passkeys differ?
MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) requires users to provide different types of authentication factors.
For example, a password plus a verification code on a mobile phone.
This is usually more secure than a password alone.
But you might ask:
“What if the attacker tricks the user into giving away the verification code too?”
This is one limitation of conventional OTP (One-Time Password) authentication.
An attacker may relay the verification code entered by the user in real time.
We therefore consider a further option:
Phishing-Resistant MFA
For example, correctly implemented FIDO2/WebAuthn authentication.

An important characteristic is that it cryptographically binds the authentication process to the legitimate website’s domain, making it difficult for a fake website to obtain a valid authentication result that can be used directly to sign in to the real website.

NIST SP 800-63B-4 explicitly states that manually entered one-time verification codes are not phishing-resistant authentication; WebAuthn can provide phishing resistance through verifier name binding. [NIST Pages](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html)

Technical clarification | Phishing resistance and multi-factor authentication are different properties. Passkeys use public-key authentication. To count as multi-factor authentication, the flow must also correctly require and verify a local activation factor such as a PIN or biometric; the FIDO2/WebAuthn name alone does not establish MFA. [NIST SP 800-63B-4, Sections 3.1.7 and 3.2.5](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html)
However, a passkey is not a universal tool that can prevent every online scam.

It primarily addresses sign-in authentication security. It cannot directly verify whether a payment request is genuine, and it certainly cannot replace an organization’s permissions and approval procedures.
The key engineering-design point
Suppose Northstar wants to improve its security. Your proposal should not simply be:
“Ask all employees to be more vigilant.”
A more complete design would be:

The company uses email-security mechanisms to filter some impersonation messages; important actions require independent verification; accounts use phishing-resistant MFA; sensitive data follows the principle of least privilege; high-risk payments require independent approval; and systems retain the necessary audit records.
These defenses complement one another, bringing the design closer to the core principle of M01-06.
6. M01-07 | How can we tell whether a phishing attack actually succeeded?
Next, switch to the perspective of a security incident investigator.
Suppose Lin at Northstar says:
“I think I clicked on a strange email yesterday.”
What should investigators do at this point?
A common mistake is to write immediately:
“Lin was targeted by a phishing attack, and his company account has been compromised.”
That conclusion may go beyond what the evidence currently supports.
SVG diagram ⑤ | Evidence levels and incident response

sourceBody.alt: CEH M09-02 / Visual diagram 05 M01-07 Incident response: do not turn “received” directly into “compromised” Separate observations, inferences and verification when assessing a security incident, and verify each level. ① Message received Verifiable evidence: Email records or a screenshot. Do not infer beyond the evidence: Only delivery is established. ② Link clicked Verifiable evidence: The user’s account and browsing history. Do not infer beyond the evidence: This does not mean malicious code was executed. ③ Credentials entered Verifiable evidence: The person’s account and login-page records. Do not infer beyond the evidence: Treat this as possible credential exposure. ④ Suspicious login Verifiable evidence: Identity-platform audit records. Do not infer beyond the evidence: This does not mean data has already leaked. ⑤ Data accessed Verifiable evidence: Access, download or exfiltration records. Do not infer beyond the evidence: Establish the content and scope. What should you do first if you suspect a phishing incident? 1 Stop suspicious actions. 2 Report to the security contact according to procedure. 3 Have the responsible person handle the account and device. 4 Preserve records and investigate the impact. Practical reminder: do not repeatedly open suspicious files yourself; recordkeeping and response must follow the organization’s authorization and procedures.

sourceBody.text: The five stages in this diagram are very important.

Diagram reading note | These five items distinguish what the available evidence establishes; they are not a fixed sequence that every incident follows. For example, an impersonated-executive payment scam may involve neither credential entry nor an unusual login. An investigation may also begin with a payment anomaly or data-access alert and work backward.
Stage 1: receiving a message
What can be confirmed is that a message was delivered to the employee.
It is not yet known whether the employee read it, clicked anything, or took any action.
Stage 2: clicking a link
If the employee says they clicked a link, record their statement and cross-check it against available browsing history and security logs.
A click alone does not mean that malicious code necessarily executed.
Stage 3: entering credentials
If the employee confirms entering a username and password on a suspicious website, treat the credentials as potentially exposed and respond immediately according to organizational procedures.
But do not automatically infer that the attacker successfully signed in.
Stage 4: discovering a suspicious sign-in
If the authentication platform shows unusual sign-in activity, investigate its source, timing, authentication method, sessions, and subsequent actions.
Note:
An “unusual sign-in” can have other explanations, such as the legitimate user using a new device or a different network.
More evidence is needed to confirm what happened.
Stage 5: data being accessed or transferred out
Suppose it is confirmed that an account downloaded company documents at an unusual time.
The next step is to investigate which documents were downloaded, how many, when, and whether there is evidence of transfer outside the organization.
State only conclusions that the evidence supports.

This principle is also consistent with MITRE ATT&CK’s approach to phishing detection: correlate email, files, process execution, network activity, and authentication records instead of drawing conclusions from a single event. [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0070/)
What should you do if you discover that you really did enter your password?
Immediately stop the suspicious activity and report it to the security contact through an established, trusted channel.

The responsible personnel should handle the account according to the risk—for example, changing the password from a trusted device, revoking suspicious sessions, checking MFA settings, and investigating relevant logs.
If a money transfer is involved, immediately contact the bank and the organization’s finance or fraud-response contact to try to stop or recover the funds.
Do not repeatedly open or run a suspicious attachment yourself just to find out whether it is malicious.
7. Connect M09-01 and M09-02 again
Now return to the main learning thread of Module 09 as a whole.
In M09-01, we already learned:
Social engineering exploits people’s trust, sense of authority, urgency, or other psychological and social factors to induce particular behaviors.
In M09-02, we see further that:
Attackers can package these psychological factors into deceptive messages through email, messaging applications, and other digital channels.
Phishing is not limited to email.
For example:
Smishing is phishing through text messages; vishing is phishing through voice calls; and quishing uses QR codes to lead users into phishing situations.
However, recognizing these names is not the most important skill.
What really matters is:
Whether the attacker uses text, voice, images, or a QR code, you can identify the message’s source, the requested action, and the relevant security boundary.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security also recommends verifying suspicious requests through an independent, trusted channel rather than using contact information provided in the suspicious message. [Canadian Centre for Cyber Security](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/dont-take-bait-recognize-and-avoid-phishing-attacks)
One more detail is worth adding:
HTTPS and a browser’s padlock icon do not mean that a website is necessarily operated by a legitimate company.
HTTPS primarily protects communication between the browser and the website it connects to; scam websites can use HTTPS too.
An encrypted connection therefore cannot replace verification of identity, domain, and transaction requests.
8. From beginner to security engineer: what judgment skills should you develop?
After today’s lesson, I hope you develop a reusable method of analysis, rather than simply remembering three English terms.
When you encounter a suspected phishing incident, start with five questions:

rows: 1. Which assets is the attacker targeting?
2. Which entry points and routes is the attacker using?
3. How is trust being exploited to induce action?
4. Which controls can block or limit the harm?
5. What evidence can establish how far the incident has progressed?

sourceBody.text: The lawful authorization and ROE (Rules of Engagement) covered in M01-03 are prerequisites that all security testing and investigations must follow.
Even a simulated phishing exercise conducted solely for training should obtain appropriate authorization in advance and establish the testing scope, data-handling methods, and reporting procedures.
The core idea most worth remembering today

Attackers exploit trust to lead people into actions that may cross security boundaries; defenders must use verification, permission controls, process design, and incident investigation to prevent or limit possible harm.
This principle applies to more than phishing.
You can continue using this way of thinking when you later study account impersonation, privilege escalation, malware, web application security, and even AI Agent Security.
9. Understanding check | Try answering in your own words
This time, we will use the original Northstar example from the teaching materials without giving the model answers first.

Website editorial addition: plain-language reference answers are provided below for self-checking, initially collapsed so you can think first. Their publication does not mean that a reader has submitted an answer or demonstrated understanding.
Scenario:
An ordinary finance staff member at Northstar receives an email.
The sender appears to be the company’s CEO. The email correctly mentions a recent teaching-materials project and asks the finance staff member to redirect a payment to a new account.
The sender also emphasizes:
“I am in a meeting right now. Do not call; just take care of it.”
At present, all that is known is that the staff member received the message. It has not been confirmed whether they transferred money as instructed.
Question A | Attack classification
If the message is confirmed to be malicious, would you classify it as phishing, spear phishing, or whaling?
Explain your reasoning, paying particular attention to the difference between “who is being impersonated” and “who is being targeted.”
Question B | Security controls
The staff member notices that the email knows the correct project name.
Does this prove that the sender really is the CEO?
If you were the company’s security engineer, how would you require the staff member to verify the request? What mechanisms would you design to reduce the risk of similar incidents?
Question C | Evidence and incident response
At present, the only fact that can be established is that the finance staff member received the message.
Can you immediately write “the company has been defrauded and lost money” in the incident investigation report?
What additional evidence do you need?
Advanced question D | Integrating knowledge across chapters
Suppose the investigation confirms that the company really did transfer money to the wrong account.
Analyze the incident using the four concepts from M01-02—Asset, Threat, Vulnerability, and Risk—then propose two improvements consistent with the defense-in-depth principle from M01-06.

sourceBody.summary: Question A reference answer | Classify by the actual target
paragraphs: Once the message is confirmed to be malicious, spear phishing is the most specific classification; it is also phishing in the broader sense. The message is tailored to a particular finance employee’s work and uses accurate project details to appear credible.

Impersonating the CEO does not by itself make this whaling. The actual target is an ordinary finance employee, not the CEO: who is impersonated and who is being deceived are different questions. It may also be a BEC-style payment scam, but any financial loss requires separate payment evidence.

sourceBody.summary: Question B reference answer | Knowing the context does not authorize the request
paragraphs: No. The project name may come from public information, leaked material, or a compromised partner account. Accurate content is a clue; it does not independently establish who is making this request or whether this payment change is approved.

Pause the account change or transfer. Use the company’s existing directory, a previously verified phone number, or an established internal system to verify the specific request with the person concerned and the authorized payment approver. Do not use new contact details, links, or reply channels supplied by the suspicious email to validate that email. “I am in a meeting” does not replace the required checks.

A process can require independent callback verification for payee-account changes and review by a separate authorized person. Systems can retain change and approval records and add suitable transfer limits or anomaly alerts. Email authentication and phishing-resistant MFA strengthen other layers but do not replace verification of the payment request itself.

sourceBody.summary: Question C reference answer | Receiving a message does not establish a loss
paragraphs: Not yet. We only know that the finance employee received a message. That does not establish a completed transfer, financial loss, or account compromise. An initial record could state: “A suspected spear-phishing message was received; changes to payment details and any actual payment remain unconfirmed.”

Preserve the original email and timestamps. Check the employee’s replies, payee-account changes, payment requests, approval records, and the bank’s actual transaction and funds status. Compare the intended payee with the actual destination. A submitted request, an approval, and a completed transfer are distinct events.

If a suspicious transfer is confirmed, promptly involve finance, security, and the bank under the organization’s procedures while preserving evidence. Whether the payment can be stopped or recovered still depends on the bank and subsequent investigation.

sourceBody.summary: Advanced question D reference answer | Connect assets, threats, vulnerabilities, and risk to defenses
paragraphs: Assets include company funds, correct payee-account data, and payment procedures and approval records. The threat is an attacker impersonating an executive to redirect a legitimate payment to an account under the attacker’s control.

Possible vulnerabilities to investigate include missing independent verification, inadequate review of account changes, or weak separation of duties. These remain hypotheses; a mistaken transfer does not prove that every control was absent. Risk concerns the likelihood and impact of misdirected funds under those conditions. The confirmed mistaken transfer is an actual event and impact, not a direct measurement of future probability.

First improvement: before changing a payee account, independently confirm the change with the genuine vendor or authorized owner through an established trusted channel, and retain the verification record. This can stop a false instruction before it enters the payment process.

Second improvement: require a separate person to review and authorize high-risk changes in the payment system, with suitable limits and immediate transaction alerts. If the earlier check fails, later approval, detection, and loss-limiting mechanisms remain. These are complementary layers, not repeated instructions to be careful.
